_instructions.about: Brain regions knowledge base for the Allen CCFv3 Mouse Brain Atlas RAG chatbot.
_instructions.how_to_add: Add entries to the 'regions' array. Each entry must have a 'structure' name that matches exactly what appears in the atlas (case-insensitive match is used). The 'parcellation_index' is optional but helps with exact lookups — find it by clicking the region in the atlas and reading the 'PARCELLATION INDEX' in the right panel.

fields.parcellation_index: Integer ID from the atlas. Find by clicking the region.
fields.structure: Structure-level name (must match atlas name exactly).
fields.substructure: Substructure name if applicable, else same as structure.
fields.function: What this region does — this is the main content the AI will use to answer questions.
fields.connectivity: Key input/output connections with other regions.
fields.clinical_relevance: Relevance to disease, disorders, or research.
fields.notes: Any extra info you want the AI to know about this region.

regions.function: The caudoputamen (striatum) is the primary input nucleus of the basal ganglia. It plays a central role in voluntary motor control, action selection, habit formation, and reward-based learning. It receives dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and glutamatergic input from the cortex and thalamus.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: cerebral cortex (glutamate), substantia nigra pars compacta (dopamine), thalamus. Outputs: globus pallidus (direct and indirect pathways), substantia nigra pars reticulata.
regions.clinical_relevance: Degeneration of dopaminergic projections to the caudoputamen is the hallmark of Parkinson's disease. Also implicated in Huntington's disease, OCD, and drug addiction.
regions.notes: In mice the caudoputamen is the rodent homologue of the primate caudate nucleus and putamen, which are separate structures in primates but fused in rodents.

regions.function: The hippocampal formation is critical for the formation of new declarative (explicit) memories, spatial navigation, and contextual learning. It encodes episodic memories and transfers them to long-term storage in the neocortex during sleep.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: entorhinal cortex (perforant path), septal nuclei, hypothalamus. Outputs: entorhinal cortex, subiculum, fornix projections to mammillary bodies and septal nuclei.
regions.clinical_relevance: One of the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease. Damage causes anterograde amnesia. Also implicated in depression, schizophrenia, epilepsy (temporal lobe seizures), and PTSD.
regions.notes: Contains distinct subregions: dentate gyrus, CA1, CA2, CA3, and subiculum, each with specialised roles in memory encoding and retrieval.

regions.function: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement, fine-tunes motor output, and maintains balance and posture. It compares intended movements with actual movements and corrects errors in real time. It also plays roles in motor learning, timing, and some cognitive functions.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts), brainstem (pontine nuclei from cortex), vestibular system, inferior olive (climbing fibres). Outputs: deep cerebellar nuclei → thalamus → motor cortex; also to brainstem and spinal cord.
regions.clinical_relevance: Damage causes ataxia (uncoordinated movement), dysmetria, and intention tremor. Implicated in autism spectrum disorder, dyslexia, and cerebellar degeneration disorders.
regions.notes: Contains more neurons than the rest of the brain combined, mostly granule cells. The Purkinje cell is its signature large output neuron.

regions.function: The isocortex (neocortex) is the largest part of the cerebral cortex and is responsible for higher-order functions including sensory perception, voluntary motor control, spatial reasoning, language, and conscious thought. It is organised into six layers and multiple functional areas.
regions.connectivity: Highly interconnected with thalamus (thalamocortical loops), other cortical areas (cortico-cortical), striatum, and brainstem. Each cortical area has specific input/output partners.
regions.clinical_relevance: Affected in stroke, traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy, and many psychiatric conditions. The specific deficit depends on which cortical area is damaged.
regions.notes: Subdivided into dozens of areas including primary motor cortex (MOp), primary somatosensory cortex (SSp), primary visual cortex (VISp), and primary auditory cortex (AUDp).

regions.function: The hypothalamus is the master regulator of homeostasis. It controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep-wake cycles, circadian rhythms, and reproductive behaviour. It also links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: limbic system, brainstem, retina (for circadian rhythms). Outputs: pituitary gland (hormones), autonomic nervous system (via brainstem and spinal cord), thalamus.
regions.clinical_relevance: Lesions cause dysregulation of body temperature, appetite (obesity or anorexia), and hormonal disorders. Implicated in diabetes insipidus, Prader-Willi syndrome, and circadian rhythm disorders.
regions.notes: Despite its small size, the hypothalamus contains numerous distinct nuclei each with specific functions, including the suprachiasmatic nucleus (master circadian clock) and arcuate nucleus (appetite regulation).

regions.function: The amygdala is the brain's threat detection and emotional processing centre. It is essential for fear conditioning, emotional memory formation, anxiety responses, and the processing of social and emotional stimuli.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: sensory cortices, thalamus (fast threat route), hippocampus, prefrontal cortex. Outputs: hypothalamus (stress hormones), brainstem (fight-or-flight), nucleus accumbens, prefrontal cortex.
regions.clinical_relevance: Hyperactivity is associated with anxiety disorders, PTSD, and phobias. Damage causes inability to recognise fear (Urbach-Wiethe disease). Also implicated in autism spectrum disorder and depression.
regions.notes: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is critical for fear learning, while the central amygdala (CeA) drives the fear response output.

regions.function: The thalamus is the brain's central relay station. Almost all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus before reaching the cortex. It also regulates consciousness, sleep, and alertness, and coordinates communication between different cortical regions.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: all sensory pathways (visual, auditory, somatosensory, taste), cerebellum, basal ganglia, brainstem, cortex. Outputs: cerebral cortex (all lobes), striatum.
regions.clinical_relevance: Damage causes sensory loss, pain syndromes (thalamic pain), sleep disorders, and disorders of consciousness. Implicated in absence epilepsy and thalamic dementia.
regions.notes: Divided into many specific nuclei: LGN (vision), MGN (audition), VPL/VPM (somatosensory), VA/VL (motor), pulvinar (attention), MD (prefrontal relay).

regions.function: Olfactory areas process smell information. Unlike other senses, olfactory signals bypass the thalamus and project directly to the olfactory cortex and limbic system, explaining the strong link between smell and emotion/memory.
regions.connectivity: Inputs: olfactory bulb (from olfactory receptor neurons in the nose). Outputs: piriform cortex, entorhinal cortex, amygdala, hypothalamus, orbitofrontal cortex.
regions.clinical_relevance: Anosmia (loss of smell) is an early symptom of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. Olfactory dysfunction is also a hallmark symptom of COVID-19.
regions.notes: The olfactory system is evolutionarily ancient and directly connects to the limbic system, which is why smells powerfully trigger emotional memories.
